title: A brain–spine interface restored control of walking after paralysis
summary: Gert-Jan Oskam used the STIMO-BSI interface to stand, walk, and climb stairs after a spinal cord injury.
account:
Gert-Jan Oskam received the STIMO-BSI brain–spine interface after an incomplete cervical spinal cord injury. The decoder translated signals from his brain into spinal stimulation. He regained control of standing and walking, including stairs and uneven ground. After 40 rehabilitation sessions, he could also walk more than 10 meters with crutches while the stimulation was off.

The researchers reported stable control for over a year, including seven months of home use. An infection required removal of one cortical implant 167 days after implantation. Rehabilitation continued after treatment, and the implant was replaced in March 2023. The report concerns one participant. On 22 October 2026, Jiang and colleagues reported in Med that a brain-spine interface restored brain-controlled leg movement on the first day after surgery in three people with motor-complete spinal cord injury in China. Their system used depth electrodes in the motor cortex, and none of the authors belong to the Lausanne team.
purpose: Researchers connected movement intentions to spinal stimulation to restore control of standing and walking.
developer: NeuroRestore (EPFL/CHUV/UNIL) with CEA-Clinatec and ONWARD Medical

ratings.reason: Life-changing benefit to one identifiable person: standing, walking, stair climbing and independent home use restored after ten years of paralysis. Some recovery persists when the device is switched off.

ai_role.statement: The REW-MSLM decoder estimated intended leg movements from cortical signals and adjusted spinal stimulation. Researchers calibrated it for the participant and set the permitted stimulation ranges.

Gert-Jan Oskam received the STIMO-BSI brain–spine interface after an incomplete cervical spinal cord injury. The decoder translated signals from his brain into spinal stimulation. He regained control of standing and walking, including stairs and uneven ground. After 40 rehabilitation sessions, he could also walk more than 10 meters with crutches while the stimulation was off.

The researchers reported stable control for over a year, including seven months of home use. An infection required removal of one cortical implant 167 days after implantation. Rehabilitation continued after treatment, and the implant was replaced in March 2023. The report concerns one participant. On 22 October 2026, Jiang and colleagues reported in Med that a brain-spine interface restored brain-controlled leg movement on the first day after surgery in three people with motor-complete spinal cord injury in China. Their system used depth electrodes in the motor cortex, and none of the authors belong to the Lausanne team.
